title: streaming-sse-chunking-backpressure-debug-notes-arjun-patel
content:
Context:
- Local repro + customer report (ACME) show intermittent stalls in streaming responses over SSE. Symptoms: initial event(s) arrive, then long pause (5-30s), then burst of remaining events (chunk coalescing). Looks like chunking/flush/backpressure issue between runtime and HTTP layer.

Timeline:
- 2024-11-05: ACME incident report, example curl session attached (below).
- 2024-11-06: Ran local repro on my laptop (macOS 13) + staging cluster. Observed same pause behavior when enabling 1s token batching.
- 2024-11-07: Pair debug with Maya/Noah. Collected tcpdumps, app logs, and nginx access logs.

Observed behavior (example):
- Client: curl -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4-mini","prompt":"stream test\n","stream":true}' \
  https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate\n
- Output: first SSE message arrives within 300ms, then 12s silence, then ~50 messages delivered back-to-back.
- No 5xx errors in app logs; request considered "healthy" by runtime.

Commands I used to repro (local/staging):
1) Raw curl SSE (repro)
   export TOKEN=...
   curl -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"model":"gpt-4-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"stream test with delay"}],"stream":true}' \
     https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate

2) Node fetch + EventSource polyfill (repro in browser env)
   // node repro.js
   import fetch from 'node-fetch'
   const res = await fetch('https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate', {
     method: 'POST',
     headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${TOKEN}`, 'Accept': 'text/event-stream', 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
     body: JSON.stringify({ model: 'gpt-4-mini', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'stream test' }], stream: true })
   });
   // pipe res.body to stdout and watch pauses

3) Python aiohttp streaming (async):
   import aiohttp, asyncio
   async def main():
     async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as s:
       async with s.post(url, headers=headers, json=payload) as r:
         async for chunk in r.content.iter_chunked(1024):
           print('CHUNK', len(chunk))

4) netcat test to isolate nginx vs app:
   # Connect directly to app port (bypass nginx)
   echo -e "POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: localhost\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\nContent-Length: ...\r\n\r\n{"model":"gpt-4-mini","stream":true}" | nc app-host 8080

What I collected:
- tcpdump (staging) shows data arriving at client but data bytes stalled for ~10s then a bunch of bytes.
- runtime logs: token flush events printed at times matching the stall/resume.
- nginx access logs show request latency > actual first byte gaps. No upstream 502.
- kernel socket buffers were not saturated (no RSTs).

Error snippets / logs:
- runtime: "INFO flush_kv_cache: flushed 0 tokens (reason=idle_timeout)\n"
- app: "DEBUG stream_chunk_sent size=512 seq=14" then nothing, then "DEBUG stream_chunk_sent size=8192 seq=15"
- client curl verbose: "< HTTP/1.1 200 OK" then no further lines until later data burst.

Hypotheses:
1) Nagle / TCP coalescing combined with small writes from runtime causing long pauses until larger write occurs. (But tcpdump shows bursts, not solely tiny packets).
2) Runtime is doing deliberate batching/flush policy (idle_timeout=100ms or 10s) that interacts poorly with SSE framing and nginx buffering.
3) nginx or ingress is buffering chunks (proxy_buffering) and only flushes when buffer fills or upstream signals end-of-stream.
4) Client-side backpressure: some Fetch/EventSource implementations do not immediately consume chunks, causing kernel to apply backpressure leading to delayed upstream writes. (Less likely: observed even with curl)
5) Chunk framing mismatch: runtime uses HTTP chunked encoding with small chunk sizes but not sending proper flushes (missing flush/syscall).

Quick experiments and results:
- Bypass nginx: reproduce persisted when hitting app directly -> suggests app/runtime is origin of pause.
- Set runtime env var STREAM_DEBUG=1 -> logs show flush events at "idle_timeout=10s" in one code path. When setting IDLE_TIMEOUT=0.1s locally, pauses dropped to ~200ms but throughput decreased (more syscalls).
- Turn off Nagle (TCP_NODELAY) on client -> no significant change.
- Increase chunk threshold in runtime (bigger coalesce buffer) -> reduced number of pauses but still saw one 3s pause.

Repro script (minimal)
- Simple looped curl to observe distribution of first-byte latency
  for i in {1..50}; do \
    curl -s -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"model":"gpt-4-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"test $i"}],"stream":true}' https://staging.api.redwood.ai/v1/generate | pv -b > /dev/null &\n    sleep 0.2
  done
- Watch tcpdump: sudo tcpdump -A -s 0 host <client-ip> and grep for "data: " lines to correlate bursts.

Notes from pairing session:
- Noah observed that the runtime path that streams from KV-cache returns small writes until it accumulates a response chunk and then writes a larger chunk. The code uses a timer to flush small pending writes. That timer default (10s) was introduced as a safety for cold-started kernels.
- Maya measured that on GKE nodes, the kernel-level coalescing plus the timer produced the observed 10s pause.

Action items / next steps:
- [P0] Short-term mitigation: lower idle flush timer in runtime to 200ms for streaming path and rollout to staging. Monitor CPU impact. (assigned: Arjun)
- [P1] Add explicit flush/syscall after writing an SSE data frame when stream-mode is enabled (investigate in runtime writer abstraction). (assigned: Noah)
- [P1] Add an e2e unit test that simulates small incremental token writes and asserts first-byte latency < 500ms. (assigned: Maya)
- [P2] Confirm nginx/proxy_buffering disabled for /v1/generate route in staging and prod; if enabled, set "proxy_buffering off" for stream endpoints. (ops)
- Collect more tcpdumps from customer environment to confirm identical pattern (requested from ACME).

Temporary workaround communicated to CS:
- Recommend using streaming=false + polling if strict real-time streaming is required and customer cannot tolerate bursts (not ideal).

Misc troubleshooting notes (for future):
- Tools: pv, tcpdump, ngrep, strace -p <pid> (watching write syscalls), ss -tin to inspect socket queues.
- When reproducing locally, keep an eye on ulimit -n and file descriptors; many concurrent curl clients can hit FD limits and change scheduler behavior.

Important log excerpts (sanitized):
- runtime: [2024-11-06T14:02:31Z] stream_writer.go:120 wrote 128 bytes
- runtime: [2024-11-06T14:02:31Z] stream_writer.go:122 pending_bytes=128 pending_count=1
- runtime: [2024-11-06T14:02:41Z] stream_writer.go:200 flush_timer fired idle_timeout=10s -> wrote 7920 bytes

If I get the okay to push the timer change to staging, I'll deploy and follow up with metrics:
- per-request first-byte delta distribution, pct50/pct90/pct99
- CPU increase on streaming nodes (expected due to syscalls)

References/links:
- Relevant code paths: runtime/pkg/streaming/stream_writer.go (TODO: add PR link after changes)
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood/inference/pull/512 (backpressure fixes, WIP)

Open questions:
- Is there any middleware between runtime and client that could be coalescing TLS records? (we saw same behavior when hitting pod IP directly, so probably not)
- Does our client SDK have any buffering layers by default? Need to audit node/python SDKs for default stream consumption behavior.

Short summary for Slack update:
- Root cause likely runtime-level flush timer + kernel coalescing -> causes 5-10s pauses for low-throughput streaming. Short-term fix: lower idle flush timer + explicit flush on SSE frames. Will validate in staging and then prod.
